CHAIR ( Senator Pratt ): I declare open this hearing of the Senate Finance and Public Administration Legislation Committee into the 2024-25 additional estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay respects to elders past and present. I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples here today. In saying those words, I must reflect on the fact that it is always a pleasure to put those words into the Hansard at every hearing, but especially on our cross-portfolio Indigenous affairs day. The committee has set 6 March 2025 as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and 24 March 2025 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. Our proceedings begin today with cross-portfolio Indigenous matters followed by the NIAA and then other agencies as listed on the program.

Under our standing orders, we must take all evidence in public, which includes answers to questions on notice. I remind witnesses that in giving evidence they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee. Such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence. The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings, which is that any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in the estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings.

I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how such policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I will incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: It's now my pleasure to welcome and acknowledge the officials at the table and the minister, Senator the Hon. Malarndirri McCarthy, Minister for Indigenous Affairs; Ms Jody Broun, chief executive officer, National Indigenous Australians Agency; Ms Tamsyn Harvey, deputy secretary, Attorney-General's Department; Ms Meg Brighton, deputy secretary, Department of Education; Ms Celia Street, acting deputy secretary, Department of Health and Aged Care; and Ms Letitia Hope, deputy secretary, Department of Social Services. It's nice to be able to acknowledge those officials representing those agencies now. We can now go to questions unless there are, of course, opening statements from those at the table, including you, Minister.

Senator McCarthy: Thank you, Chair. I acknowledge the Ngambri and Ngunnawal people and thank the committee and the agency and all those who are attending today in advance for their presence and being able to comply with the invitation to the committee.

CHAIR: Thank you, Minister.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Thank you all for attending today. It's most appreciated, given that this is our last Senate estimates, I imagine, before the election is called. Being mindful of the looming election, I would like to ask that, where possible, answers be provided today and not on notice. If that means officials can come back later today with those answers, that would be preferred. Whilst cross-portfolio agencies and the NIAA are here, I would like to ask for an explanation regarding the dismal return of answers to questions on notice. All of the parliamentary departments' questions on notice were answered on time. Prime Minister and Cabinet had 739 out of 750. The Department of Finance had 130 out of 156. Cross-portfolio Indigenous matters had only one out of 1,630 questions answered on time. As at 24 January, there were still 525 questions outstanding. I would like to have an explanation for this. I understand that there's probably a prioritisation in terms of those questions, but how can it be that only one question is answered on time?

Mr Jamble : We look to answer questions as soon as possible when they are received by the committee. We manage the questions on behalf of the Indigenous portfolio bodies as well. As soon as we are able to develop the responses, we send them through to the minister's office. Senate order No. 21, which was tabled a couple of weeks ago, has the dates relevant to that. Once we receive the clearance, we table those.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Receive clearance from whom?

Mr Jamble : From the minister and the minister's office in line with the guide for witnesses.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Are you suggesting that your responses are provided to the minister's office on time, and clearance then comes from—

Mr Jamble : I can go through the dates that we provided those to the minister. We did have a delay in getting some of those questions, noting that we had 1,600 questions to answer.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: How many of those answers to the 1,630 questions were provided on time to the minister's office?

Mr Jamble : I don't have that specific number, but I can tell you the dates they were provided, if that's helpful. I'll come back with that in the next little while. It's just not right here. On 11 November, we had one. On 22 November, we had 42. On 25 November, we had 17. On 26 November, we had three. On 29 November, we had 88. On 2 December, we had 66. On 3 December, we had 27. On 4 December, we had 17. On 5 December, we had one. On 6 December, we had six. On 9 December, we had 32. On 10 December, we had 416. On 11 December, we had three. On 12 December, we had 220. On 13 December, we had 46. On 16 December, we had 11. On 17 December, we had 131. On 18 December, we had 399. On 19 December, we had 10. On 6 January, we had two. On 7 January, we had 62. Somewhere in that—I'll just double-check—the cut-off date was 19 December. I can do the maths in a minute and let you know which ones were before and after.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Thank you. Minister, is it usual practice for the agencies to provide all answers to cross-portfolio Indigenous matters to your office before they are published?

Senator McCarthy: I understand that it is.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Minister, can you explain the delay, then, in publishing those answers by the due date since they were provided to your office?

Senator McCarthy: Well, we had 1,600 questions. That is the largest number of any department across government.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Minister, surely one question on time was provided in response—

Senator McCarthy: If I may respond, please—

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: out of that many.

Senator McCarthy: If I may respond.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: This is a bit of an insult.

Senator McCarthy: If I may respond.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Please do.

Senator McCarthy: Yes. Thank you. We has 1,600 or more questions, which is more than any other department or agency across government. I commend the agency and all those involved with trying to get those answers in on time. We have and had completed all those answers. We may not have met the due date for every single question in terms of the load of questions that we received, but I would say that you have had them at least 10 days or more before the estimates. I thank all involved for the amount of work that has gone into those questions being answered.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: So it's usual practice, then, for questions to be provided by the minister's office to be published for the purpose of Senate estimates—

Senator McCarthy: Well, if you look at the standing orders, you will see that every minister has to table the QONs. I thought you would know that as shadow minister.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Certainly. I didn't expect that they would be provided at the 11th hour for the benefit of—

Senator McCarthy: It's not the 11th hour. Ten days before estimates does give plenty of time.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: One answer was provided. I guess it's better than last time. Can a representative from the NIAA, Attorney-General's, Health, Social Services and Education please tell me on what date before the due date they provided answers to the minister? That might have to be provided by the end of the day, perhaps. How many answers did they provide to the minister before the due date? I'll take that one on notice for some time during the day. I have a couple of questions regarding the Justice Reinvestment Unit. The Justice Reinvestment Unit was meant to be up and running in the middle of last year. At supplementary estimates, we were advised that it would be up and running by the end of 2024. Can we get an update as to whether it's up and running yet?

Ms Woods : I can confirm that the Justice Reinvestment Unit has been established within the Attorney-General's Department.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Can you tell me when it commenced?

Ms Woods : In February.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Of the $12.5 million budgeted for the unit's design, how much of that has been spent?

Ms Woods : Part of the $12.5 million is apportioned to justice reinvestment support in establishing both the unit as well as the Justice Reinvestment Program. In terms of expenditure for the unit itself beyond this point, $382,852 is budgeted through to the end of the financial year. In terms of the establishment of the unit, a portion of the total funding was utilised to support the establishment of the Justice Reinvestment Program. I am trying to find the costs for you. I might take that on notice. I will be able to provide it back to you. I just can't find it in the brief at the moment.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Was the annual budget $382,000?

Ms Woods : No. That's just pro rata until the end of this financial year. In terms of the ongoing budget for the interim unit—sorry, I have given you the amount for 2024-25. For 2025-26, it is budgeted for $1.203 million. Ongoing from 2026-27, it is $2.588 million annually.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: How many people are employed in the unit?

Ms Woods : At the moment, there are six ASL in the unit, which is six people. When the unit transitions to the final Justice Reinvestment Unit in 2026-27, it will increase to 10.5 FTE.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Are the positions in the unit existing positions transferred from existing departments, or are they new positions?

Ms Woods : I guess it's a bit of both in the sense that they are newly created positions, but the ASL has transferred out of the existing Justice Reinvestment branch.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Can you outline the executive structure?

Ms Woods : Of the Justice Reinvestment Unit? It's headed by an SES officer, who is actually present today. I can ask the head of the unit to come to the table as needed. There are two EL1s and three APS staff.

Ms Turk : We have me, as the assistant secretary, and two EL1s and three APS staff in the branch.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Do they report to you within the unit?

Ms Turk : Yes.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Now that the unit is up and running, how will the administration of the program change?

Ms Bogaart : The unit will be providing two key functions. The first will be to provide support to communities to progress their justice reinvestment initiatives. It will also be developing a monitoring and evaluation framework. The program itself will continue to be administered within the Attorney-General's Department by government. So the unit won't be administering funding. I think we've discussed this in previous estimates.

Senator LIDDLE: I have a couple of questions related to your area of responsibility. It relates to the justice partnership. I have been speaking to a number of women's legal services. Many of them are Aboriginal community controlled or are operating in areas where most of their clients are Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. They don't seem to appreciate the government's claims that there is an increase in funding to their services. They raise the issue of indexation and inflation and say in real terms their funding has not increased, including additional organisations transitioning into the pool. Are you able to explain to me whether there is additional funding in that pool but only because there are more organisations in that pool or have those organisations had an increase in funding in real terms?

Ms Bogaart : I need to clarify your question. Are you talking about family violence prevention and legal services under the National Access to Justice Partnership?

Senator LIDDLE: Yes. You could talk about those. Can you talk more generally?

Ms Bogaart : You just said women's legal services run by Aboriginal community controlled organisations. I'm just clarifying. I can speak about the National Access to Justice Partnership, which commences on 1 July this year. The family violence prevention and legal services are currently funded by the NIAA. They will be transitioning to AGD. I can talk about from 1 July. NIAA will need to speak to anything in the current financial year. I can tell you that from 1 July funding for family violence and prevention legal services will increase by 112 per cent on their current funding over the five years of the NAJP. There will continue to be the 16 FVPLSs. We haven't increased or decreased the number of services that will be providing services under the NAJP. It's a 112 per cent increase in funding with the same number of services.

Senator LIDDLE: In that funding pool? You are bringing 16 services into that funding pool.

Ms Bogaart : There are already 16 services. Their funding will be $366.8 million over the five years of the NAJP. That is a $193.4 million increase from their current funding levels over the previous five years.

Senator LIDDLE: Can you explain why they keep telling me that they are actually not advantaged at all by this new funding?

Ms Bogaart : I'm not sure. I think a 112 per cent increase is a reasonably substantial increase. It was provided following the National Cabinet meeting on 6 September in recognition of increasing funding, particularly for legal assistance services for DV.

Senator LIDDLE: Is that all services?

Ms Bogaart : There are several different subsectors in the NAJP. There are legal aid commissions. There are women's legal services. There are community legal centres. There are Aboriginal legal services. There are the family violence and prevention legal services.

Senator LIDDLE: I'm trying to understand. Does that mean that every service in that pool got an increase in funding, or were they selected on the basis of need?

Ms Bogaart : Every single subsector received an increase. The increase is slightly different depending on the subsector. Community legal centres, including women's legal services, had a 74 per cent increase in funding over five years. The Aboriginal legal services received a 64 per cent increase. Legal aid commissions received a 24 per cent increase.

Senator LIDDLE: I want to ask you about the data that actually informs how you work out funding distributions and where demand might actually peak. For example, when we saw the alcohol restrictions lifted in Central Australia and the removal of the CDC, in those areas there was a spike in incidents of family violence. Are you able to support an acute response? You fund them for their general operational activities. What happens when essentially what is unfortunately a norm in their everyday lives is basically amplified and exacerbated by a policy decision, as in this case?

Ms Guivarra : In addition to what Ms Bogaart has said in relation to the new National Access to Justice Program, there was a recognition, actually, of the need to provide additional funding to our family violence and prevention legal services this current year. In May 2024, we provided an additional $8.6 million. That was done basically to ensure pay parity and workforce stabilisation. For the current financial year, they are receiving $47.6 million. We recognised, obviously through evidence, including through the Mundy review of the national legal assistance programs, that there was a need to provide additional funding to family violence and prevention legal services and women's legal services. That has contributed to, as Ms Bogaart said, the significant increase in funding that they will receive under the National Access to Justice Program, which won't commence, of course, until this year.

Senator LIDDLE: So will they get their money on 1 July, because that's the issue they've been raising, which is the uncertainty around new funding? Will they get their money on 1 July? Is that set in stone?

Ms Bogaart : The NAJP is a national partnership. That means that the Commonwealth provides the funding to the states and territories. All the states and territories have signed the NAJP, so the funding will flow for the states to distribute. The states are working really quite intensively with all of the providers under the NAJP, not just the FVPLSs, to ensure that they will have funding from 1 July. All providers have also received a letter of assurance either from the NIAA for the FVPLS or from the states and territories that they will get at least their minimum amounts that they are getting now with decisions about additional funding currently being worked through each state and territory process. They've all got different processes of how they do that.

Senator LIDDLE: Thank you. That's helpful.

CHAIR: Senator Liddle, I will need to rotate the call shortly. I will allow the coalition to keep the call, but I have senators on this side seeking the call as well.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: I have just one more question in relation to the Justice Reinvestment Unit. The government's 2022 election commitment states, 'An Albanese Labor government will commit $79 million, matched by the states, to expand justice reinvestment initiatives across the country, helping to turn the tide on incarceration and deaths in custody.' Has that $79 million been matched by the states?

Ms Bogaart : We are working with the states and territories on how we can co-fund initiatives. We have some justice reinvestment collaboration principles that have been agreed through the Standing Council of Attorneys-General. We're in the process of negotiating MOUs with the states and territories that do have justice reinvestment projects in their jurisdiction. In terms of co-funding, there are a couple of projects around the country where we are working with the states and territories. For example, the project on Groote Eylandt is jointly funded by the Northern Territory government, AGD and the NIAA. Some of the projects are in very early stages. As they progress, we will continue to work with the states and territories for co-funding.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: To date, the $79 million hasn't been matched?

Ms Bogaart : There hasn't been a formal matching.

Senator NAMPIJINPA PRICE: Thank you. I will pass the call.

Senator STEWART: My questions go to the economic empowerment work. In October last year, I was very happy to have Minister McCarthy come to Melbourne during Indigenous Business Month. We had a round table of various First Nations businesses that are absolutely kicking goals for their families and communities. In the same week, I attended the AITC tourism conference at the MCG. I heard again about the incredible work being done by our mob to celebrate our culture and identity and inviting lots of people in to share in that experience. The opportunity for businesses in tourism has been described in the First Nations businesses succeeding internationally report published in August 2024. I have done some work in this space for a committee that I chair. It is really important that we do work to support First Nations businesses and support entrepreneurs to be able to launch their businesses. I think the work the government is undertaking in this space is really positive and great. One example of it is the legislation to enhance the ability for IBA, Indigenous Business Australia, to remove barriers for IBA borrowing money and partnering with private capital and governments. I want to understand the change. How could it support unlocking First Nations business and economic empowerment? Why is it important for businesses that we're doing this?

Ms Persson : I might start and hand over to my colleague Shane Dexter. As part of the Future Made in Australia package, royal assent was granted for this bill back in February. The amendments, as you mentioned, provide Indigenous Business Australia with borrowing powers. It enables them to raise capital to allow investment in First Nations individuals, communities and businesses around the country. It provides essentially First Nations people with more opportunities to start and grow a business. The amendments also give IBA flexibility to pursue a range of opportunities with government and private partners to support First Nations economic development. For example, partnering with the NAIF is one of those opportunities. At the moment, we're working with our central agencies and IBA to develop the rules that will sit around that.

Senator STEWART: Can you give us an example of what an Aboriginal business might want to do?

Mr Dexter : Thank you for the question. My colleague has just outlined some of the barriers that previously existed for IBA in its legislative framework. It wasn't able to borrow or raise capital.

Senator STEWART: Why was that an issue?

Mr Dexter : It created a limitation on the capital that IBA has available to it to coinvest with Indigenous businesses. The National Indigenous Australians Agency uses the IBA to run the business support program, which provides concessional loans for Indigenous businesses, particularly at the start-up and pre-bank phase. They also provide home loans, which my colleague can talk to. Obviously, the resources that are available to IBA are limited by the appropriation that is made available to them. Allowing them to borrow and to raise capital allows them to significantly increase those resources that can be put towards both those business growth activities and the home loan space.

Ms Persson : I might add to that. For example, in the NAIF and some of those organisations, their criteria are set for larger businesses. Our First Nations businesses miss out. This legislative change provides IBA with the opportunity to partner with them and to borrow with them and provide those opportunities for First Nations businesses.

Senator STEWART: Correct me if I am wrong: is one of the issues that this is seeking to solve the fact that lots of Aboriginal businesses, I suppose, experience discrimination and a whole bunch of barriers in being able to borrow through mainstream lenders the capital required to expand their businesses? I think the Grants Committee's final meeting was in June that year, but the board decided on 24 April to abolish the Grants Committee completely.

Senator LIDDLE: Having policies which are recommended in here is one thing, but that's pretty 101 in governance—not having people with a declared conflict of interest actually making recommendations for whether businesses and other projects should be funded. Have you done a check of your entire organisation and its policies and processes since? I know that there has been a change in the organisation to make sure that there is no transition of these kinds of issues, which, for an organisation with $680 million, just shouldn't be in existence.

Mr Werro: We actually wrote a conflict-of-interest policy in April or May last year. We did that with the Australian Government Solicitor. We also put together a training program off the back of that, with the Australian Government Solicitor, to cover gifts, benefits and hospitality as well. We've also updated a lot of our governance policy suites, including our procurement policy and our recruitment policy, to make sure that everything that's in the conflicts policy is actually reflected throughout all the other policies that we have, and we've put some training in place for staff and for board and committee members as well.

Senator LIDDLE: What, in your processes and your systems, actually gives you the confidence that you can push back on badly behaving board members to make sure that none of this can occur?

Mr Werro: As I said, the committee that was where the problems were has gone. The chair—

Senator LIDDLE: Have all the people that were on that committee gone?

Mr Werro: Yes, they have, apart from the board members that sat on that.

Senator LIDDLE: Apart from the board members? So the board members that sat on that committee are still in the organisation? Is that what you're telling me?

Mr Werro: I'll need to check that and come back to you, but I believe the whole committee was dissolved. I can check the membership here. One second.

Mr Wyborn: There were two committee members that were also board members. Since the committee was dissolved, those two committee members are continuing board members.

Senator LIDDLE: They're continuing board members?

Mr Wyborn: Correct. I will come back on notice to confirm that.

Senator LIDDLE: So two people who were actually on that committee, who were board members at the time, remain in the corporation as board members when they were making decisions about projects where they had a declared conflict of interest already. It's pretty extraordinary.

Mr Wyborn: Those board members weren't necessarily the members that also had conflicts of interest, but we'd be happy to take that on notice to confirm that and bring that back to you.

Senator LIDDLE: Okay.
